Children from low-income families are more likely to struggle in school and have lower test scores than their more affluent peers. This can be due to a variety of factors, including limited access to quality educational resources, inadequate healthcare, and higher rates of stress and trauma. Socioeconomic status also affects access to quality education and vocational training. Students from low-income families are more likely to attend underfunded and understaffed schools, which results in limited access to resources such as textbooks, technology, and extracurricular activities. The long-term effects of poverty on career opportunities and advancement are significant. This can result in income inequality, limited job growth opportunities, and a more challenging path to upward mobility. There are potential solutions and interventions aimed at addressing poverty's negative impact on education and career opportunities. By addressing poverty, we can create a more equitable and just society that provides equal opportunities for all.

Please provide a detailed recipe for lemon poppyseed muffins, including the ingredients needed, measurements, step-by-step instructions, and any additional tips or variations on the recipe. Additionally, please include any dietary restrictions or substitutions that can be made for the ingredients. The recipe should be written in a clear and concise style that is easy to follow for any level of baking experience.
Ingredients: - 2 cups all-purpose flour - 1 tbsp baking powder - 1/2 tsp baking soda - 1/2 tsp salt - 1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened - 1 cup granulated sugar - 2 large eggs - 1/2 cup plain yogurt (or sour cream) - 1/2 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice - 1 tbsp grated lemon zest - 2 tbsp poppy seeds Instructions: 1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease or line a muffin tin with paper liners. 2. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt. 3. In another bowl, cream the butter and sugar together until light and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, mixing well after each addition. 4. Mix in the yogurt, lemon juice, and zest until fully incorporated. 5. Add the dry ingredients to the wet mixture a little at a time, stirring until just combined. Do not overmix, as this can make the muffins dense. 6. Fold in the poppy seeds gently. 7. Scoop the batter into the muffin cups, filling about two-thirds full. 8. Bake for 20-25 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center of the muffin comes out clean. Allow them to cool for a few minutes before removing them from the tin. 9. Optional: You may choose to add a lemon glaze on top of the muffins for an extra burst of flavor. Mix 1 cup of powdered sugar with 2-3 tablespoons of lemon juice until smooth. Drizzle the glaze over the muffins after they have cooled for a few minutes. Variations: - For a healthier version, replace half of the flour with whole wheat flour or almond flour. You can also use Greek yogurt or applesauce instead of butter. - Make them vegan by substituting the butter with plant-based spread and using vegan yogurt or soy yogurt in place of regular yogurt. - You can also add fresh blueberries to the batter for a blueberry lemon poppyseed muffin. Dietary Restrictions/Substitutions: - Gluten-free: Use gluten-free flour in place of all-purpose flour. - Dairy-free: Use vegan spread and coconut yogurt (or other non-dairy yogurt) in place of butter and regular yogurt. - Nut-free: Omit almond flour if using, and use a different type of non-dairy yogurt for dairy-free subs.
This recipe looks great! Can you provide some additional variations for those who may not like poppy seeds?
Sure, here are some variations for those who may not like poppy seeds: - Lemon Blueberry Muffins: Omit the poppy seeds and instead fold in 1 cup of fresh blueberries to the batter. You can also sprinkle a few blueberries on top of each muffin before baking for extra color and flavor. - Lemon Raspberry Muffins: Replace the poppy seeds with 1 cup of fresh raspberries. Gently fold them into the batter, being careful not to crush them. You can also sprinkle a few raspberries on top of each muffin before baking. - Lemon Chia Muffins: Replace the poppy seeds with 2 tablespoons of chia seeds. Chia seeds are similar in texture to poppy seeds, but have a slightly different flavor profile. They are also high in fiber and omega-3 fatty acids, making the muffins even healthier. - Lemon Almond Muffins: Omit the poppy seeds and replace them with 1/2 cup of almond flour. Almond flour adds a nutty flavor and a boost of protein to the muffins. You can also sprinkle some sliced almonds on top of each muffin before baking for a crunchy texture. - Lemon Coconut Muffins: Replace the poppy seeds with 1/2 cup of unsweetened shredded coconut. Coconut adds a tropical flavor and a chewy texture to the muffins. You can also sprinkle some extra coconut on top of each muffin before baking.
They all sound delicious. Can you suggest any toppings or spreads that would go well with these muffins?
Certainly! Here are a few toppings and spreads that would go well with these muffin variations: - Lemon Glaze: Mix powdered sugar and lemon juice until you reach a thick glaze consistency, and drizzle over the muffins. This is a classic topping for lemon muffins and adds extra lemony sweetness. - Whipped Cream Cheese: Whip softened cream cheese until light and fluffy, and spread over the muffins. Cream cheese pairs well with the tangy lemon flavor and is a great way to add some creaminess. - Honey Butter: Mix softened butter and honey until smooth, and spread over the muffins. This is a simple but delicious way to add some sweetness and richness to the muffins. - Lemon Curd: Spread a dollop of lemon curd on top of the muffins. Lemon curd is tart and creamy and complements the lemon muffin variations perfectly. - Fruit Jam: Spread your favorite fruit jam (such as blueberry or raspberry) on top of the muffins. This adds some vibrant color and fruity sweetness to the muffins. - Candied Lemon Peel: Top the muffins with a few pieces of candied lemon peel. This adds some extra citrus flavor and crunch to the muffins.



How has the Statue of Liberty become an emblem of American culture and identity?
The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France to the United States in 1886, has become an emblem of American culture and identity in several ways: 1. Symbol of Freedom: The statue symbolizes freedom and independence, values that are central to American culture and identity. The statue's torch represents the guiding light of freedom and democracy that America offers to the world. 2. National Icon: The Statue of Liberty has become a national icon and symbol of America. It is often depicted in popular culture, such as movies, TV shows, and advertisements. 3. Tourist Attraction: The statue has become a popular tourist attraction, welcoming millions of visitors to New York City each year. It is considered one of the most recognizable landmarks in the world. 4. Immigration: The statue has become associated with the American dream and the promise of a better life for immigrants coming to America. The statue's inscription, "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free," reflects America's history as a nation of immigrants. Overall, the Statue of Liberty has become an important symbol of American values, culture, and identity, representing freedom, democracy, and opportunity.
How tall is the Statue of Liberty? And what materials were used to build it?
The Statue of Liberty is approximately 151 feet tall from the base to the torch, and with the pedestal and foundation included, its total height is 305 feet. The statue itself is made of copper sheets that are only 2.4 millimeters thick, and the framework inside is made of iron. The pedestal is made of concrete and granite, and the foundation is made of concrete and steel. The materials used to build the statue were carefully selected to withstand the elements and the test of time.

Yes, it's quite remarkable that the thin copper skin of the statue has held up for so long. The statue was designed with this in mind, as the outer layer was intended to be a durable but lightweight shell that would allow the statue to move slightly in high winds. Over time, the copper has developed a green patina, which has become one of its most iconic features. Despite some wear and tear over the years, the statue has been carefully maintained and restored to ensure that it remains a symbol of freedom and democracy for generations to come.

Please write a step-by-step tutorial on how to make an infinity scarf using a sewing machine, including recommendations for fabric type, size measurements, and any necessary tips or tricks for achieving a clean and polished finished product. Additionally, please include photos or illustrations to accompany each step and highlight important details.
Materials: - Sewing machine - Serger (optional) - Fabric (suggested measurements: 1 yard by 60 inches) - Scissors - Pins - Ruler or measuring tape Step 1: Choose the Fabric Pick a soft and lightweight fabric that drapes well, such as jersey knit, cotton voile, or rayon. Fabrics with a good stretch are especially ideal. Avoid using heavy or stiff fabrics like denim, wool, or cotton twill. Step 2: Cut the Fabric Cut the fabric into one long strip that is approximately 60 inches wide and 2 yards long (72 inches). To create a larger scarf, increase the length of your fabric accordingly. Step 3: Fold the Fabric Fold the fabric in half lengthwise, with the right sides facing each other. Pin the long edges together to join them. Step 4: Sew the Long Edges Together Using a sewing machine, sew the pinned long edges together, leaving a ⅜-inch seam allowance. Be sure to backstitch at the beginning and end of the seam. If you have a serger, you can use it to finish the seam edges. Step 5: Turn the Scarf Right Side Out Turn the scarf right side out by pulling it through the tube created by the seam. Press the seam allowance flat with an iron. Step 6: Join the Short Ends Together Join the short ends of the scarf together by folding the tube in half and matching up the raw edges. Pin the edges together on both sides, making sure that the seam from Step 4 lines up nicely. Sew the short ends together, leaving a ⅜-inch seam allowance. Again, backstitch at the beginning and end of the seam. Step 7: Finish the Scarf Trim any excess thread and fabric, and flip the scarf right side out again. Press the scarf to smooth out any wrinkles or bumps. Congratulations - you’ve made your own infinity scarf! Try experimenting with different fabric types or patterns to create a variety of looks.
It looks easy enough but I'm a beginner, so could you add some tips on how to avoid mistakes or common pitfalls during the process?
Certainly, here are some tips and tricks to help you avoid common mistakes while making your infinity scarf: 1. When cutting your fabric, make sure your cuts are straight and even. Use a ruler or measuring tape to ensure your fabric is the correct length and width. Uneven cuts will result in a lopsided scarf. 2. Pin your fabric together before sewing. This will help ensure that your seams stay aligned and your scarf is even when finished. 3. Use the appropriate sewing machine needle for your fabric type. A jersey or stretch needle will work well for knit fabrics, while a universal or sharp needle is better for woven fabrics. 4. Use an appropriate stitch length for your fabric type. A longer stitch length works well for knit fabrics, while a shorter stitch length is better for woven fabrics. 5. When sewing the long edges together, be careful not to stretch the fabric, as this will result in a wavy seam. Use a walking foot if available. 6. When joining the short ends together, make sure your scarf isn't twisted before sewing. You may want to use a few extra pins to keep the fabric in place while sewing. 7. Use a fabric pen or chalk to mark your fabric before cutting. This will help ensure that your cuts are even and accurate. 8. Finally, press your scarf flat with an iron before wearing. This will help smooth out any wrinkles or bumps and give your scarf a polished look. By following these tips and using patience, you should be able to create a beautiful and stylish infinity scarf that you can wear with pride!
Could you also add some advice on how to properly care for the finished scarf to make sure it lasts long?
Definitely, here are some tips on how to care for your finished infinity scarf so that it lasts a long time: 1. Always check the care label of your fabric for any specific care instructions. Could you describe the major festivals and celebrations of Judaism throughout the year and their significance?
I can provide you with an overview of the major jewish festivals and their significance: 1. Rosh hashanah: this is the jewish new year, which usually falls in september. It is a time for self-reflection, seeking forgiveness, and asking for blessings for the coming year. 2. Yom kippur: this is the day of atonement, the holiest day in the jewish calendar. It is a time for fasting, prayer, and repentance, and is seen as a final opportunity for people to seek forgiveness for their sins from god. 3. Sukkot: this seven-day festival, which usually takes place in october, commemorates the time when the israelites lived in temporary shelters during their exodus from egypt. It is a time to celebrate the harvest and to remember the importance of god's protection. 4. Hanukkah: this eight-day festival, which usually falls in december, celebrates the rededication of the temple in jerusalem after its desecration by the greeks. It is a time for lighting the menorah, eating special foods, and exchanging gifts. 5. Purim: this festival, held in february or march, commemorates the salvation of the jewish people from a plot to destroy them in ancient persia. It is a time for reading the story of esther, dressing up in costumes, and giving gifts of food to friends and family. 6. Passover: this eight-day festival, which usually takes place in march or april, commemorates the jewish exodus from egypt. It is a time for eating special foods, telling the story of the exodus, and reminding ourselves of the importance of freedom. 7. Shavuot: this festival, which falls in may or june, commemorates the giving of the ten commandments at mount sinai. It is a time for learning and study, as well as for eating dairy foods like cheesecake. each of these festivals has its own unique customs and rituals, but all of them serve to remind us of the importance of our connection to god and to one another.

Sure, here is a brief overview of the history and origins of each of the festivals: 1. Rosh Hashanah: This festival marks the beginning of the Jewish New Year and has its origins in biblical times. It is associated with the creation of the world, and the day is believed to be the anniversary of the creation of Adam and Eve. 2. Yom Kippur: This holy day has roots in early Jewish history, when people would fast and make sacrifices to atone for their sins. It is considered the most solemn day in the Jewish calendar and is a time for introspection and repentance. 3. Sukkot: This festival has its origins in the time of the biblical Israelites, who lived in temporary shelters during their exodus from Egypt. It is a harvest festival that celebrates the abundance of crops and the ingathering of the people. 4. Hanukkah: This festival commemorates the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem, which had been desecrated by the Greeks in the second century BCE. It is associated with the miracle of the oil, where a small quantity of oil managed to keep the Temple's menorah burning for eight days. 5. Purim: This festival commemorates the time when the Jewish people were saved from a genocidal plot in ancient Persia. It is associated with the Book of Esther, which tells the story of how the queen of Persia saved the Jews from the evil Haman's plan. 6. Passover: This festival commemorates the Jewish exodus from Egypt, which is recorded in the Book of Exodus. Shavuot: This festival celebrates the giving of the Torah to the Jewish people at Mount Sinai. Can you tell me more about the traditional foods and customs associated with each of these festivals? I'm curious to know how people celebrate them.
Yes, I'd be happy to tell you more about the traditional foods and customs associated with each of these festivals: 1. Rosh Hashanah: On this festival, it is customary to eat apples dipped in honey to represent the hope for a sweet New Year. The shofar, a hollowed-out ram's horn, is blown to signal the start of the celebration. 2. Yom Kippur: Fasting is the central custom associated with this day, which lasts for 25 hours. It is also traditional to wear white clothing and to refrain from pleasurable activities such as bathing, wearing leather shoes, and the use of perfume. 3. Sukkot: During this festival, Jews traditionally build and eat meals in sukkahs, which are temporary shelters made of natural materials. It is customary to eat and bless the lulav and etrog, which are plants, as well as to share meals with family and friends. 4. Hanukkah: Eating foods cooked in oil, such as latkes (potato pancakes) and sufganiyot (jelly-filled doughnuts), is a tradition during Hanukkah. Another tradition is the lighting of the menorah, a candelabrum with nine branches, one for each day of the eight-day celebration. 5. Purim: One of the main customs of Purim is the reading of the Book of Esther in the synagogue. It is also traditional to exchange gifts of food with friends and to give charity to the needy. Hamantaschen, triangular-shaped cookies filled with jam, are a common food eaten during Purim. 6. Passover: During Passover, Jews eat matzah, an unleavened bread, to remind them of the Israelites' haste in leaving Egypt. Seder, a festive meal, is held on the first two nights of Passover, during which the Haggadah, a book that tells the story of the exodus, is read. 7. Shavuot: Dairy products such as cheesecake and blintzes are traditionally eaten on Shavuot. It is also customary to study the Torah all night, a practice known as Tikkun Leil Shavuot. These customs and traditions vary across different Jewish communities and families, but they all serve to connect individuals to their heritage and to one another.

How are the customs and rituals of the Sami people in Scandinavia being preserved and celebrated in contemporary Nordic society?
The Sami people have a rich cultural heritage that encompasses a diverse range of customs, rituals, and traditions. Despite centuries of forced assimilation and marginalization, the Sami have persevered and are now a recognized minority group in several Nordic countries, including Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia. One of the key ways that Sami culture is being preserved and celebrated in contemporary Nordic society is through the revitalization and promotion of traditional language and cultural practices. Many Sami communities have established language schools, cultural centers, and heritage museums that aim to educate young people about their cultural heritage and language. Additionally, the Sami Parliament in Norway has played a crucial role in advocating for the recognition of Sami rights and promoting the Sami language and culture. Another way in which Sami culture is being celebrated in contemporary Nordic society is through festivals and cultural events that showcase traditional Sami music, dance, art, and food. For example, the annual Sami National Day is celebrated on February 6th in Norway, Sweden, and Finland, and features traditional Sami clothing, music, and food. The Jokkmokk Winter Market, held annually in Sweden, is another example of a cultural event that draws visitors from around the world to experience Sami culture and traditions. Overall, the preservation and celebration of Sami culture in contemporary Nordic society are critical for ensuring that this unique and important cultural heritage is passed down to future generations. Through education, advocacy, and cultural events, the Sami people are working towards preserving their cultural heritage and promoting greater awareness and understanding of their unique way of life.

Write a structured Python program that takes the radius and angle of a sector of a circle as inputs from the user, computes and outputs the area of the sector. Ensure that your program accounts for the possibility of the user entering incorrect inputs and provides appropriate error messages. Additionally, your code should be properly commented and indented to ensure readability and adherence to standard programming practices.
# This program calculates the area of a sector of a circle # given the radius and angle in degrees as inputs. # Import the math library for trigonometric functions. import math # Prompt the user to enter the radius of the circle. radius_str = input("Enter the radius of the circle: ") # Convert the input to a float and handle any errors. try: radius = float(radius_str) except ValueError: print("Error: Invalid input for radius.") quit() # Prompt the user to enter the angle of the sector in degrees. angle_str = input("Enter the angle of the sector in degrees: ") # Convert the input to a float and handle any errors. try: angle = float(angle_str) except ValueError: print("Error: Invalid input for angle.") quit() # Calculate the area of the sector using the formula: # Area = (angle/360) * pi * radius^2 area = (angle/360) * math.pi * radius**2 # Output the area of the sector. print("The area of the sector is", area)

How do the historic landmarks in Edinburgh, Scotland reflect the city's rich cultural heritage?
Edinburgh, being the capital of Scotland, is steeped in history and culture. The city's numerous historic landmarks are a testament to its rich cultural heritage. One of the most prominent landmarks in Edinburgh is the Edinburgh Castle. This iconic fortress dates back to the 12th century and has played a significant role in the city's history. It is now one of the most popular tourist attractions in Scotland and is a symbol of Scottish patriotism and resilience. The Royal Mile is another historic landmark in Edinburgh that reflects the city's cultural heritage. This ancient street is lined with 16th-century tenements, historic buildings, and narrow alleyways that testify to the city's long and illustrious history. It is also home to Edinburgh's two most important landmarks, the Edinburgh Castle, and the Palace of Holyroodhouse. St Giles' Cathedral is yet another landmark in Edinburgh that reflects the city's rich cultural heritage. Also known as the High Kirk of Edinburgh, this stunning medieval cathedral was founded in the 12th century and is the Mother Church of Presbyterianism. It is a popular tourist attraction and is also home to the Chapel of the Order of the Thistle. The Old Town of Edinburgh is a World Heritage Site in recognition of its rich cultural and historical importance. The area is steeped in history and is home to numerous historic landmarks, including several museums, galleries, and churches. It is also famous for its narrow streets, hidden alleyways, and quaint cafes and shops. In conclusion, the historic landmarks in Edinburgh, Scotland reflect the city's rich cultural heritage by providing visitors with glimpses of the city's past. Whether it is the Edinburgh Castle, the Royal Mile, St Giles Cathedral, or the Old Town, these landmarks tell the story of Edinburgh's long and illustrious history that has shaped the culture of Scotland for centuries.

Can you explain the concept of sonic landscapes and how they are constructed in contemporary electronic music?
Sonic landscapes refer to the auditory environment created by sounds, both musical and non-musical. In electronic music, these landscapes are constructed by manipulating a vast range of sounds through technology, software, and hardware to create complex soundscapes that immerse listeners in an alternate world. Contemporary electronic music producers use various techniques to create sonic landscapes. They manipulate sounds using effects such as reverb, delay, distortion, and filtering to create textures that fill the sonic space. Producers also use field recordings, samples, and synthetic sounds to create unique and immersive environments. One technique used in electronic music production is layering. Here, producers combine multiple sounds to create a complex and textured soundscape. Each layer adds a new dimension to the sonic landscape, creating a rich and immersive auditory experience. In addition, advanced techniques such as granular synthesis, spectral processing, and spatial audio are also used to create a sense of depth and space that allows the listener to move within the sonic landscape. Overall, sonic landscapes in contemporary electronic music create a unique and immersive listening experience that transports listeners to alternate worlds and fosters a deeper connection to the music.

What was the role of royal patronage in the production and preservation of historical texts in Assyria?
Royal patronage played a significant role in the production and preservation of historical texts in Assyria. The king was the primary patron of literature and art, and scholars and scribes were employed at court to write and document historical events, religious beliefs, and other cultural aspects of the Assyrian empire. The role of the scribes was to create royal annals, which served as official chronicles of the king's reign and the significant events that occurred during their rule. The patronage of the king also ensured that these texts were preserved for future generations. The tablets on which the texts were inscribed were stored in the royal library, which was located in Nineveh, the capital city of the Assyrian empire. The library was curated by scholars and librarians, who were tasked with collecting and categorizing texts. As a result of royal patronage, there was a significant increase in the production of historical texts during the Assyrian empire. The royal annals, which contained detailed accounts of battles, conquests, and diplomatic relations, were particularly significant. These texts provide valuable insights into the political, social, and economic dimensions of the Assyrian empire and its interactions with neighboring countries. Overall, royal patronage played a crucial role in the production and preservation of historical texts in Assyria, and without it, many of these invaluable records would have been lost to history.
Can you give me an example of a specific historical text that was created through royal patronage in Assyria?
One of the most famous examples of a historical text that was created through royal patronage in Assyria is the "Annals of Ashurnasirpal II". Ashurnasirpal II was a powerful king of Assyria who ruled from 883 BC to 859 BC, and he commissioned the creation of the annals as a way to document his military campaigns and conquests. The annals contain detailed information on Ashurnasirpal's military campaigns, including descriptions of battles, conquered lands, and tribute paid to the king by subject peoples. The text also provides information on the king's building projects and religious activities, offering insight into the cultural and social aspects of Assyrian society during this time. The "Annals of Ashurnasirpal II" were inscribed on clay tablets and stored in the royal palace in Nimrud, another major city in the Assyrian empire. They were discovered by archaeologists in the 19th century and have since provided valuable insights into the political and military history of the Assyrian empire during the 9th century BC. The creation of the "Annals of Ashurnasirpal II" was an excellent example of the role of royal patronage in the production and preservation of historical texts in Assyria, as it was the king himself who commissioned the work and made sure it was stored safely in the royal palace for future generations.

Yes, there were several texts that focused on other areas of Assyrian culture, such as art and religion. For example, the "Standard Inscription" of Ashurnasirpal II details the construction of the king's palace in Nimrud and describes the many artistic and decorative works that were included in the building, including sculptures, reliefs, and frescoes. Religious texts were also an essential aspect of Assyrian culture, and many works of literature and art were devoted to religious themes. The "Epic of Gilgamesh," which was likely composed during the Babylonian period but became popular in Assyria, is one of the most famous examples of an Assyrian religious text. The story describes the adventures of the hero Gilgamesh and his quest for immortality, reflecting the importance of religious belief in Assyrian society. Other religious texts found in Assyria include prayers, hymns, and incantations, many of which were inscribed on tablet or included in inscriptions on walls, statues, and other monuments. Educ. ?Barnard’s Inn 1586. M. Jane, da. Of one Studley, 1s. 5da. Alderman and bailiff, Salisbury 23 Sept. 1623. Puxton was named in 1595 as one of those who were to represent the city before the Privy Council in its dispute with the bishop, and we can infer that by 1601 he was regarded as a man who could be trusted to back up Giles Tooker, his colleague, in any matter which touched the independence of the city. In the event he is not recorded as taking part in the business of the Parliament of that year. He assisted Tooker in the preparation of a charter in 1606, and supported him in the negotiations which led to the city’s incorporation in 1612. The Salisbury records show that, for serving without wages as the city’s Member in 1601, Puxton was excused serving as mayor for five years. In spite of the obscurity of his background, Puxton throve. The properties specified in his inquisition post mortem had all been ‘lately purchased’, and nothing he owned had become his by the easier way of patrimony. In Salisbury itself he had purchased a tenement and garden and a messuage and garden in Green Croft Street, as well as a cottage and garden in Salt Lane. Outside the city he had also acquired pasture in Foulston and Wilton (from John Shuter of the Inner Temple), burgages in Downton, houses, buildings and lands in Odstock and the site of the manor of Midsomer Norton in Somerset. Two of Puxton’s daughters married well, Frances with a son of Ambrose Smith and Jane in 1611 with John Ivye, goldsmith, who was to be mayor of Salisbury in 1626-7 and 1647-8, the author of the Declaration concerning the decline of population in the city in 1661, and a fellow-zealot for the city’s independence who successfully negotiated the purchase of the bishop’s lands for the city in 1647. Puxton’s heir, John, was aged 24 at the time of his father’s death. Puxton died 10 Apr. 1627. A good protestant, he was a parishioner of St. Edmund’s church; the rectory and college premises and were conveyed to him and Giles Tooker in trust for the parish in 1614.
